newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Landless peasants march into Brazilian capital.
newsitem.headline: Landless peasants march into Brazilian capital.

text.p: Landless peasants marched into the Brazilian capital on Thursday to demand speedier land reforms and justice for slain colleagues in the biggest protest faced by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
About 1,500 members of the radical Landless Movement (MST) arrived in Brasilia carrying rusty farm tools and waving red flags after a 750-mile (1,200-km) march.

"Millions of people have been forced off the land and now live in poverty. They need to get back to their roots in the countryside," march organiser Cleide Santos Rebello said as the demonstrators advanced towards the presidential palace.

The marchers were due to join thousands of trade union members, civil servants, teachers and unemployed workers who oppose Cardoso's plans to privatise state companies and cut thousands of public sector jobs.

The protest also marked the first anniversary of the killing by police of 19 landless peasants. The massacre shocked Brazilians and spurred Cardoso to declare land reform a priority of his government.
No one has been arrested in connection with the killings and the MST says the government has not done enough to speed up the transfer of vacant farmland to the landless.
The Catholic Church joined in the criticism of Cardoso, who is increasingly under fire for failing to match low inflation with improved social conditions.
"The impoverishment of the people cannot be accepted as the inevitable price of economic development," Brazil's National Bishops Conference (CNBB) said in a statement.

The document called for the suspension of the upcoming $5 billion privatisation of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce and criticised lawmakers for setting a $10,000 cap on their monthly income while millions of workers surive on a minimum wage of $105.
"The violence that permeates all of society is also a consequence of economic policies that created one of the world's most unfair income distributions," the document said.

Cardoso has said his government has helped 13 million Brazilians overcome poverty and its target of settling 280,000 landless families in four years represents Brazil's most ambitious land reform programme to date.

He remains a firm favourite to win next year's presidential race but public opinion also backs the peasants. A recent poll said 85 percent of Brazilians back the MST's controversial policy of invading unused farmland. The plight of the landless was also a theme of a popular television soap opera.

Cardoso was due to meet with MST leaders on Friday, the first top-level meeting between the government and the movement since last August. Officials said on Wednesday the government might widen its target for settling families if the MST agrees to stop invading land.
